after:
_Introduction and plan of the work_

Each nation's annual labour is the original source of all the necessities and comforts it consumes in the course of a year. These consist either of the direct produce of that labour or of what it buys from other nations with that produce.

How well the nation is supplied therefore depends on how much of that produce, or what it buys, there is for the number of people who have to consume it.

In every nation this proportion is determined by two things. The first is the skill, dexterity and judgement with which people generally apply their labour. The second is the proportion between the number engaged in useful work and the number who are not. Whatever the soil, climate or extent of a particular country, the abundance or scarcity of its annual supplies must, in its particular circumstances, depend on these two things.

The first seems to matter more than the second. Among the hunting and fishing peoples described as savage, everyone able to work does some useful labour, endeavouring to provide as well as possible for himself and those of his family or tribe who are too old, young or infirm to hunt or fish. Yet such peoples are so miserably poor that mere want often drives them, or at least leaves them believing that they are driven, either to kill their infants, their old people and their chronically sick outright, or to leave them to starve or be devoured by wild animals. In civilised and flourishing nations, in contrast, many people do no work at all. Many of them consume the produce of ten, often a hundred, times as much labour as most of the people who work. Yet the whole society produces so much that there is often plenty for everyone. A worker of the poorest and lowest rank, if thrifty and industrious, may enjoy a greater share of the necessities and comforts of life than anyone among those other peoples can obtain.

The first book of this inquiry considers what has made labour so much more productive and how its produce is naturally distributed among people of different ranks and circumstances in society.

So long as the skill, dexterity and judgement with which a nation applies its labour remain the same, the abundance or scarcity of its annual supplies must depend on the proportion between those employed in useful labour each year and those who are not. As will appear later, the number of useful and productive workers is everywhere proportionate to the amount of capital used to put them to work and to the way that capital is employed. The second book therefore examines what capital is, how it is gradually accumulated and how much labour it sets in motion when used in different ways.

Nations fairly well advanced in the skill, dexterity and judgement with which they work have followed very different policies in directing labour as a whole. Those policies have not all been equally favourable to the size of its produce. Some nations have particularly encouraged rural industry, others the industry of towns. Scarcely any nation has dealt impartially with every kind. Since the fall of the Roman Empire, European policy has been more favourable to the crafts, manufactures and commerce of towns than to agriculture, the industry of the countryside. The third book explains how this policy seems to have begun and taken hold.

These different policies may originally have sprung from the private interests and prejudices of particular groups, with no thought or foresight of their consequences for the general welfare. Yet they have given rise to very different theories of political economy. Some exalt the importance of industry in the towns, others that of industry in the countryside. These theories have considerably influenced both learned opinion and the public conduct of princes and sovereign states. In the fourth book I have tried to explain, as fully and distinctly as I can, these various theories and their principal effects in different times and nations.

The purpose of the first four books is to explain what the income of the people as a whole consists of, or what funds have supplied their annual consumption in different times and nations. The fifth and last book examines the revenue of the sovereign or commonwealth. First I ask what expenses a sovereign or commonwealth must incur, which should be paid for by contributions from the whole society, and which by particular parts or members of it. Second, I examine the different ways the whole society can be made to contribute to the expenses that fall on it as a whole, and the main advantages and disadvantages of each. Third and last, I ask what reasons have led nearly all modern governments to mortgage part of this revenue or incur debts, and what effect those debts have had on the real wealth of society, its annual produce of land and labour.

_Book I. What improves the productive powers of labour, and how its produce is naturally distributed among the different ranks of the people_

The Division of Labour

before: Over the course of the last century, taking one year with another, grain was dearer in both parts of the United Kingdom than during the present one. This is a fact that can no longer be reasonably doubted, and the proof is, if anything, even more decisive for Scotland than for England. In Scotland it rests on the public fiars — annual valuations, made on oath according to the actual state of the markets, of every sort of grain in every county of Scotland. If such direct proof needed any backing, I would add that the same has held in France, and probably in most of Europe. For France the proof is perfectly clear. But while it is certain that in both parts of the United Kingdom grain was somewhat dearer in the last century than now, it is equally certain that labour was much cheaper. So if the labouring poor could raise their families then, they must be much more comfortable now. In the last century the most usual day-wages for common labour across most of Scotland were sixpence in summer and fivepence in winter. Three shillings a week — very nearly the same rate — is still paid in parts of the Highlands and Western Isles. Across most of the Lowlands the most usual wage for common labour is now eightpence a day; tenpence, sometimes a shilling, around Edinburgh, in the counties bordering England — probably because of that nearness — and in a few other places where the demand for labour has lately risen considerably, around Glasgow, Carron, Ayrshire, and so on. In England, improvements in farming, manufacturing, and trade began much earlier than in Scotland. The demand for labour, and hence its price, must have risen with them. So in the last century as in the present, wages were higher in England than in Scotland. They have also risen considerably since then, though, because of the greater variety of rates paid in different places, it is harder to say by how much. In 1614 a foot soldier's pay was the same as today, eightpence a day. When the rate was first set, it would naturally have been pegged to the usual wage of common labourers, the class from which foot soldiers are usually drawn. Lord Chief Justice Hales, writing in the reign of Charles II, reckons the necessary cost of a labourer's family of six — father, mother, two children able to do something, and two who cannot — at ten shillings a week, or twenty-six pounds a year. If they cannot earn this by their labour, he supposes, they must make it up by begging or stealing. He seems to have looked into the matter very carefully. (See his scheme for the maintenance of the poor in Burn's History of the Poor Laws.) In 1688 Mr Gregory King, whose skill in political arithmetic Dr Davenant praises so highly, reckoned the ordinary income of labourers and out-servants at fifteen pounds a year per family, which he took to consist on average of three and a half persons. So his figure, though it looks different, comes very nearly to the same thing at bottom as Judge Hales's. Both put the weekly cost of such families at about twentypence a head. Both the cash income and the cash expense of such families have risen considerably since then through most of the kingdom — more in some places, less in others — though perhaps almost nowhere as much as some exaggerated accounts of present wages have lately led the public to believe. It must be noted that the price of labour can nowhere be pinned down very precisely, since different rates are often paid in the same place for the same kind of work, not only according to the worker's differing skill but according to the easiness or harshness of the employer. Where wages are not fixed by law, all we can claim to determine is what the most usual rates are; and experience seems to show that the law can never set them properly, however often it has pretended to.

before: First, wages vary with how easy or hard the work is, how clean or dirty, and how honourable or dishonourable. In most places, taking the year as a whole, a journeyman tailor earns less than a journeyman weaver, because his work is much easier. A journeyman weaver earns less than a journeyman smith, because, although the work is not always easier, it is much cleaner. A journeyman blacksmith, though a skilled craftsman, seldom earns as much in twelve hours as a collier, who is only a labourer, earns in eight; the collier's work is dirtier, more dangerous, and carried on in daylight above ground. Honour makes up a large part of the reward in every honourable profession, which, in pure money terms and all things considered, are generally underpaid, as I shall try to show later. Disgrace works the opposite way. Butchering is a brutal and hateful trade, yet in most places it is more profitable than most ordinary trades. The most detestable employment of all, that of public executioner, is, relative to the amount of work done, better paid than any ordinary trade whatever.

before: In ancient times, before any charities of this kind had been set up to educate poor people for the learned professions, the rewards of eminent teachers appear to have been far greater. Isocrates, in what is called his discourse against the sophists, reproaches the teachers of his own day with inconsistency. "They make the most magnificent promises to their scholars," he says, "and undertake to teach them to be wise, to be happy, and to be just; and, in return for so important a service, they stipulate the paltry reward of four or five minae." "Those who teach wisdom," he goes on, "ought certainly to be wise themselves; but if any man were to sell such a bargain for such a price, he would be convicted of the most evident folly." He certainly does not mean here to overstate the reward, and we may be sure it was no less than he says. Four minae came to thirteen pounds six shillings and eightpence; five minae to sixteen pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence. So something not less than the larger of those two sums must at that time have been the usual pay of the most eminent teachers at Athens. Isocrates himself charged ten minae, or 33 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence, from each scholar. When he taught at Athens he is said to have had a hundred scholars. I take this to be the number he taught at one time, or who attended what we would call one course of lectures; a number that will not seem extraordinary for so great a city and so famous a teacher, who taught, what is more, what was then the most fashionable of all subjects, rhetoric. He must therefore have made, from each course of lectures, a thousand minae, or 3,335 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence. A thousand minae is in fact named by Plutarch, in another passage, as his didactron, or usual fee for teaching. Many other eminent teachers of those times appear to have amassed great fortunes. Gorgias made a present to the temple of Delphi of a statue of himself in solid gold. We must not, I suppose, imagine it was life-size. His manner of living, like that of Hippias and Protagoras, two other eminent teachers of the time, is portrayed by Plato as splendid, even to the point of ostentation. Plato himself is said to have lived with a good deal of magnificence. Aristotle, after serving as tutor to Alexander, and being most generously rewarded, as everyone agrees, by both him and his father Philip, still thought it worth his while to return to Athens to take up teaching at his school again. Teachers of the sciences were probably less common in those days than they became an age or two later, when competition had probably somewhat reduced both the price of their labour and the admiration for their persons. Yet the most eminent of them seem always to have enjoyed a standing far above any of their profession today. The Athenians sent Carneades the Academic and Diogenes the Stoic on a solemn embassy to Rome; and although their city had by then declined from its former greatness, it was still an independent and considerable republic.

before: But the relative values of these two kinds of food, bread and butcher's meat, differ greatly at different stages of agriculture. In its crude beginnings, the unimproved wilds, which then make up by far the greater part of the country, are all given over to cattle. There is more butcher's meat than bread, so bread is the food most competed for and consequently fetches the highest price. At Buenos Aires, Ulloa tells us, four reals, twenty-one and a half pence sterling, was forty or fifty years ago the usual price of an ox chosen from a herd of two or three hundred. He says nothing about the price of bread, probably because he found nothing remarkable about it. An ox there, he says, costs little more than the labour of catching it. But corn cannot be grown anywhere without a great deal of labour, and in a country lying on the River Plate, at that time the direct route from Europe to the silver mines of Potosi, the money price of labour could be very cheap. It is otherwise once cultivation has spread over the greater part of the country. Then there is more bread than butcher's meat. The competition shifts direction, and the price of butcher's meat comes to exceed that of bread.

before: In 1262, the 51st year of Henry III, an ancient statute called the assize of bread and ale was revived, which the king says in the preamble had been made in the time of his forebears, some of them kings of England. It is probably, then, at least as old as his grandfather Henry II, and may be as old as the Conquest. It regulates the price of bread according to whatever the price of wheat happens to be, from one shilling to twenty shillings the quarter in the money of those days. But statutes of this kind are generally assumed to provide with equal care for all departures from the middle price, those below it as well as those above. Ten shillings, then, containing six ounces of silver, Tower weight, and equal to about thirty shillings of our present money, must on this assumption have been reckoned the middle price of the quarter of wheat when this statute was first passed, and must have remained so in the 51st year of Henry III. We cannot, therefore, be far wrong in supposing that the middle price was not less than a third of the highest price at which this statute regulates the price of bread, that is, six shillings and eightpence of the money of those days, containing four ounces of silver, Tower weight.

before: Indeed, until the price of cattle has reached this height, it seems scarcely possible that even most of the land capable of the highest cultivation can be fully cultivated. On all farms too far from a town to bring manure from it—that is, on by far the greater part of those in any large country—the amount of well-cultivated land must be in proportion to the amount of manure the farm itself produces, and this in turn must be in proportion to the stock of cattle kept on it. The land is manured either by pasturing the cattle on it or by feeding them in the stable and carting their dung out to it. But unless the price of cattle is enough to pay both the rent and the profit of cultivated land, the farmer cannot afford to pasture them on it, and still less can he afford to feed them in the stable. Cattle can be fed in the stable only with the produce of improved and cultivated land, because gathering the scanty, scattered produce of waste and unimproved land would take too much labour and be too costly. So if the price of cattle is not enough to pay for the produce of improved and cultivated land when they are allowed to pasture on it, that price will be even less able to pay for that produce when it has to be gathered with a good deal of extra labour and carried into the stable to them. In these circumstances, then, no more cattle can be fed in the stable at a profit than are needed for tillage. But these can never supply enough manure to keep constantly in good condition all the land they are capable of cultivating. What they do supply, being not enough for the whole farm, will naturally be saved for the land where it can be applied most profitably or conveniently—the most fertile, or perhaps that nearest the farmyard. This land will therefore be kept constantly in good condition and fit for tillage. The rest will, for the most part, be left to lie waste, producing scarcely anything but some wretched pasture, just enough to keep alive a few straggling, half-starved cattle; the farm, though much overstocked compared with what its full cultivation would require, is very often overstocked compared with its actual produce. A portion of this waste land, however, after being pastured in this miserable way for six or seven years together, may be ploughed up, when it will perhaps yield a poor crop or two of bad oats or some other coarse grain; then, being completely exhausted, it must be rested and pastured again as before, while another portion is ploughed up, to be in the same way exhausted and rested again in its turn. Such, indeed, was the general system of management all over the low country of Scotland before the Union. The land kept constantly well manured and in good condition seldom exceeded a third or a fourth of the whole farm, and sometimes did not amount to a fifth or a sixth of it. The rest was never manured, yet a certain portion of it was, all the same, regularly cultivated and exhausted in turn. Under this system, plainly, even that part of Scotland's land capable of good cultivation could produce but little compared with what it might be capable of producing. But however disadvantageous this system may appear, before the Union the low price of cattle seems to have made it almost unavoidable. If, despite a great rise in the price, it still prevails through a considerable part of the country, this is in many places no doubt due to ignorance and attachment to old customs, but in most places to the unavoidable obstacles which the natural course of things sets against the quick establishment of a better system: first, the poverty of the tenants, who have not yet had time to acquire a stock of cattle large enough to cultivate their land more fully—the same rise in price that would make it worth their while to keep a larger stock making it harder for them to acquire it; and secondly, their not having yet had time to put their land in condition to maintain this larger stock properly, even supposing they could acquire it. The increase of stock and the improvement of land are two things that must go hand in hand, neither of which can much outrun the other. Without some increase of stock there can be scarcely any improvement of land, but there can be no considerable increase of stock except as a result of a considerable improvement of land, since otherwise the land could not maintain it. These natural obstacles to the establishment of a better system can be removed only by a long course of thrift and industry; and half a century, or perhaps a century more, must pass before the old system, which is gradually wearing out, can be wholly abolished throughout all the different parts of the country. Of all the commercial advantages Scotland has gained from the Union with England, this rise in the price of cattle is perhaps the greatest. It has not only raised the value of all Highland estates but has perhaps been the main cause of the improvement of the low country.

The rest will, for the most part, be left to lie waste, producing scarcely anything but some wretched pasture, just enough to keep alive a few straggling, half-starved cattle; the farm, though much understocked compared with what its full cultivation would require, is very often overstocked compared with its actual produce. A portion of this waste land, however, after being pastured in this miserable way for six or seven years together, may be ploughed up, when it will perhaps yield a poor crop or two of bad oats or some other coarse grain; then, being completely exhausted, it must be rested and pastured again as before, while another portion is ploughed up, to be in the same way exhausted and rested again in its turn. Such, indeed, was the general system of management all over the low country of Scotland before the Union. The land kept constantly well manured and in good condition seldom exceeded a third or a fourth of the whole farm, and sometimes did not amount to a fifth or a sixth of it. The rest was never manured, yet a certain portion of it was, all the same, regularly cultivated and exhausted in turn. Under this system, plainly, even that part of Scotland's land capable of good cultivation could produce but little compared with what it might be capable of producing. Without some increase of stock there can be scarcely any improvement of land, but there can be no considerable increase of stock except as a result of a considerable improvement of land, since otherwise the land could not maintain it. These natural obstacles to the establishment of a better system can be removed only by a long course of thrift and industry; and half a century, or perhaps a century more, must pass before the old system, which is gradually wearing out, can be wholly abolished throughout all the different parts of the country. Of all the commercial advantages Scotland has gained from the Union with England, this rise in the price of cattle is perhaps the greatest. It has not only raised the value of all Highland estates but has perhaps been the main cause of the improvement of the low country.

before: I have not been able to find any such authentic records for the price of raw hides in ancient times. But this does not seem to have been the case with raw hides. Fleetwood, however, from an account in 1425 between the prior of Burcester Oxford and one of his canons, gives us their price, at least as stated on that particular occasion, namely: five ox hides at twelve shillings; five cow hides at seven shillings and threepence; thirty-six sheep skins of two years old at nine shillings; sixteen calf skins at two shillings. In 1425, twelve shillings contained about the same quantity of silver as twenty-four shillings of our present money. An ox hide, therefore, was in this account valued at the same quantity of silver as 4s. ⅔ of our present money. Its nominal price was a good deal lower than at present. But at six shillings and eightpence the quarter, twelve shillings would in those times have bought fourteen bushels and four-fifths of a bushel of wheat, which at three and sixpence the bushel would at present cost 51s. 4d. before: Any rise in the money price of goods that came entirely from a fall in the value of silver would affect all kinds of goods equally and raise their prices across the board, by a third, or a fourth, or a fifth, according as silver happened to lose a third, a fourth, or a fifth of its former value. But the rise in the price of provisions, which has been the subject of so much reasoning and conversation, does not affect all kinds of provisions equally. Even those who explain this rise by a fall in the value of silver admit that, taken on average over the present century, the price of corn has risen much less than the price of some other provisions. before: Pennsylvania was always more moderate in issuing paper money than any other of our colonies. Accordingly its paper currency is said never to have sunk below the value of the gold and silver current in the colony before its first issue of paper. Before that issue the colony had raised the denomination of its coin, and had by act of assembly ordered 5s. sterling to pass in the colony for 6s:3d., and afterwards for 6s:8d. So a pound in colony currency, even when that currency was gold and silver, was more than thirty per cent. below the value of £1 sterling; and when that currency was turned into paper, it was seldom much more than thirty per cent. below that value. The excuse for raising the denomination of the coin was to prevent the export of gold and silver, by making equal quantities of those metals pass for larger sums in the colony than in the mother country. It was found, however, that the price of all goods from the mother country rose exactly in proportion as the denomination of the coin was raised, so that their gold and silver were exported as fast as ever.

before: In each of these periods, however, there was not only much private and public wastefulness, many expensive and needless wars, and a great diversion of the annual produce from supporting productive people to supporting unproductive ones; but sometimes, amid the chaos of civil strife, there was such utter waste and destruction of stock as might be supposed not only to slow down — as it certainly did — the natural accumulation of riches, but to have left the country poorer at the end of the period than at the beginning. So in the happiest and most fortunate of all these periods, the one since the Restoration, how many disorders and misfortunes have occurred which, had they been foreseen, would have been expected to bring not just impoverishment but the total ruin of the country: the Fire and the Plague of London, the two Dutch wars, the disorders of the Revolution, the war in Ireland, the four expensive French wars of 1688, 1701, 1742, and 1756, together with the two rebellions of 1715 and 1745. In the course of the four French wars the nation has run up more than £145,000,000 of debt, over and above all the other extraordinary annual expense they caused, so that the whole cannot be reckoned at less than £200,000,000. So large a share of the annual produce of the country's land and labour has, since the Revolution, been used on various occasions to support an extraordinary number of unproductive people. But had those wars not given this particular direction to so large a capital, most of it would naturally have been used to support productive people, whose labour would have replaced, with a profit, the whole value of what they consumed. The value of the annual produce of the country's land and labour would have been considerably increased by it every year, and every year's increase would have increased still further that of the following year. More houses would have been built, more land improved, and land already improved better cultivated; more manufactures would have been set up, and those already set up extended further; and how high the real wealth and income of the country might by now have risen, it is perhaps not very easy even to imagine.

before: Land held by such tenants is really cultivated at the proprietor's expense, just as much as land worked by slaves. There is, however, one crucial difference between them. These tenants, being free men, can acquire property, and since they receive a fixed share of the land's produce, they have an obvious interest in making the whole produce as large as possible, so that their own share will be large too. A slave, by contrast, who can gain nothing but his upkeep, looks after his own comfort by making the land yield as little as possible beyond that upkeep. It was probably partly because of this advantage, and partly because of the encroachments that the sovereigns, always wary of the great lords, gradually encouraged their serfs to make against the lords' authority, encroachments that seem at least to have made this kind of servitude thoroughly inconvenient, that villeinage gradually died out across most of Europe. The exact time and manner in which so important a change came about is one of the most obscure points in modern history. The Church of Rome claims great credit for it, and it is certain that as early as the twelfth century, Alexander III issued a bull for the general emancipation of slaves. This, however, seems to have been more a pious exhortation than a law demanding strict obedience from the faithful. Slavery went on almost everywhere for several centuries afterwards, until it was gradually abolished by the combined working of the two interests just mentioned, that of the proprietor on one side and that of the sovereign on the other. A serf, once freed and at the same time allowed to keep possession of the land, having no capital of his own, could work it only with what the landlord advanced to him, and so must have been what the French call a metayer.

before: In a country with no foreign trade and none of the finer manufactures, a man with £10,000 a year can hardly spend his income on anything other than maintaining, say, a thousand families, all of whom are therefore at his command. In present-day Europe, a man with £10,000 a year can spend his whole income, and generally does, without directly maintaining twenty people or being able to command more than ten footmen who are hardly worth commanding. Indirectly, though, he probably maintains as many people as before, or even more. For although the quantity of luxury goods he exchanges his entire income for is very small, the number of workers employed in producing and preparing those goods must have been very large. Their high price generally comes from the wages of that labour and the profits of all the employers along the way. By paying that price, he indirectly pays all those wages and profits, and so indirectly helps maintain all those workers and their employers. Yet he generally contributes only a very small share to each one: perhaps not a tenth to a very few, not a hundredth to many, and to some not even a thousandth or a ten-thousandth of their whole yearly upkeep. So although he helps maintain them all, they are all more or less independent of him, because they can generally be maintained without him.

before: It may not bear directly on the present subject, but I cannot help noting that very old families, those who have held a sizeable estate from father to son for many generations in succession, are very rare in commercial countries. By contrast, in countries with little commerce, such as Wales or the Scottish Highlands, they are very common. Arabian histories seem to be full of genealogies, and there is a history written by a Tartar Khan, translated into several European languages, that contains hardly anything else, which proves that ancient families are very common among those nations. In countries where a rich man can spend his income only by maintaining as many people as it will support, he tends to overspend, and his generosity, it seems, is rarely fierce enough to make him try to maintain more than he can afford. But where he can spend the greatest income on himself alone, he often sets no limit on his spending, because he often sets no limit on his vanity or his fondness for himself. In commercial countries, therefore, riches very rarely stay long in the same family, despite the harshest laws aimed at preventing their dispersal. Among simple nations, by contrast, they often do stay, without any laws to that effect; for among shepherd nations like the Tartars and Arabs, the perishable nature of their property makes any such laws impossible.

before: This sequence, however, runs against the natural course of things, and so it is necessarily both slow and uncertain. Compare the slow progress of those European countries whose wealth depends largely on their commerce and manufactures with the rapid advance of our North American colonies, whose wealth rests entirely on agriculture. Across most of Europe the population is not thought to double in less than five hundred years. In several of our North American colonies it is found to double in twenty or twenty-five years. In Europe, the law of primogeniture and various forms of entail prevent the breaking up of great estates and so hinder the multiplication of small landowners. Yet a small landowner who knows every inch of his little property, regards it with all the affection that property, especially small property, naturally inspires, and on that account takes pleasure not just in cultivating it but in adorning it, is generally the most industrious, intelligent, and successful improver of all. Those same laws, besides, keep so much land off the market that there are always more capitals looking to buy than there is land to sell, so whatever is sold always fetches a monopoly price. The rent never covers the interest on the purchase money, and is burdened on top of that with repairs and other occasional charges to which interest on money is not subject. Buying land is, everywhere in Europe, a most unprofitable way to use a small capital. For the sake of greater security, a man of moderate means who retires from business will sometimes choose to put his small capital into land. A professional man, too, whose income comes from another source, often likes to secure his savings the same way. But a young man who, instead of going into trade or a profession, put a capital of two or three thousand pounds into buying and cultivating a small piece of land might indeed expect to live very happily and very independently, but he must say goodbye forever to any hope of great fortune or great distinction, which a different use of his money would have given him the same chance of winning as anyone else. Such a person, moreover, though he cannot aspire to be a great landowner, will often scorn to be a mere farmer. So the small amount of land brought to market, and the high price of what is brought, keeps a great deal of capital from being employed in cultivation and improvement that would otherwise have gone that way. In North America, by contrast, fifty or sixty pounds is often found to be enough capital to start a plantation. There, buying and improving uncultivated land is the most profitable use of the smallest as well as the greatest capital, and the most direct road to all the fortune and distinction the country can offer. Such land in North America can indeed be had almost for nothing, or at a price far below the value of its natural produce, which is impossible in Europe or in any country where all the land has long been private property. If landed estates in Europe were divided equally among all the children whenever a landowner died leaving a large family, the estate would usually be sold. So much land would come to market that it could no longer fetch a monopoly price. The free rent of the land would come no closer to covering the interest on the purchase money, and a small capital could be employed in buying land as profitably as in any other way.

When the necessities of life have been taxed in a country, they claim, it becomes proper to tax not only the same necessities imported from abroad but all sorts of foreign goods that could compete with anything produced by domestic industry. Subsistence, they say, necessarily becomes dearer as a result of such taxes, and the price of labour must always rise with the price of the labourer's subsistence. before: From the start of the winter fishery of 1771 to the end of the winter fishery of 1781, the tonnage bounty on the herring-buss fishery stood at thirty shillings a ton. before: Sugar was originally an enumerated commodity, which could be exported only to Great Britain; but in 1751, on a petition from the sugar-planters, its export was permitted to all parts of the world. The restrictions under which this freedom was granted, however, combined with the high price of sugar in Great Britain, have made it largely ineffective. Great Britain and her colonies still continue to be almost the sole market for all the sugar produced in the British plantations. Their consumption is rising so fast that, although the import of sugar has greatly increased over the last twenty years thanks to the growing improvement of Jamaica and the ceded islands, the export to foreign countries is said to be not much greater than before.

before: The enumerated commodities are of two kinds. First, those that are either peculiar to America, or cannot be produced, or at least are not produced, in the mother country. Of this kind are molasses, coffee, coconuts, tobacco, pimento, ginger, whalefins, raw silk, cotton, wool, beaver and other peltry of America, indigo, fustic, and other dye-woods. Secondly, those that are not peculiar to America but are, and can be, produced in the mother country, though not in quantities sufficient to supply most of her demand, which is chiefly met from foreign countries. Of this kind are all naval stores, masts, yards, and bowsprits, tar, pitch, and turpentine, pig and bar iron, copper ore, hides and skins, and pot and pearl ashes. The largest possible import of commodities of the first kind could not discourage the growth, or interfere with the sale, of any part of the mother country's produce. By confining them to the home market, our merchants, it was expected, would not only be able to buy them cheaper in the plantations, and so sell them at a better profit at home, but to establish between the plantations and foreign countries a profitable carrying trade, of which Great Britain would necessarily be the centre or emporium, being the European country into which those commodities were first to be imported. The import of commodities of the second kind might also be managed, it was supposed, so as to interfere not with the sale of the same kinds produced at home, but with that of the kinds imported from foreign countries; because, by means of suitable duties, they could be made always somewhat dearer than the home-produced kind, and yet a good deal cheaper than the foreign kind. So by confining such commodities to the home market, the aim was to discourage the produce not of Great Britain but of certain foreign countries with which the balance of trade was believed to be unfavourable to Great Britain.

before: That a slave's condition is better under an arbitrary government than under a free one is, I believe, borne out by the history of every age and nation. In Roman history, the first time we read of a magistrate stepping in to protect a slave from his master's violence is under the emperors. When Vidius Pollio, in the presence of Augustus, ordered one of his slaves who had committed a slight fault to be cut to pieces and thrown into his fish pond to feed his fish, the emperor angrily commanded him to free at once not only that slave but all the others he owned. Under the republic, no magistrate could have had the authority to protect the slave, much less to punish the master.

before: The exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to lessen, or at least to hold below what it would otherwise rise to, both the enjoyments and the industry of all those nations in general, and of the American colonies in particular. It is a dead weight on the action of one of the great springs that sets a large part of the business of mankind in motion. By making colonial produce dearer in all other countries, it reduces how much of it is consumed, and so cramps the industry of the colonies, along with both the enjoyments and the industry of all other countries, which enjoy less when they pay more for what they enjoy, and produce less when they get less for what they produce. By making the produce of all other countries dearer in the colonies, it cramps in the same way the industry of all other colonies, and both the enjoyments and the industry of the colonies. It is a clog that, for the supposed benefit of a few particular countries, hampers the pleasures and burdens the industry of all other countries, and of the colonies more than of any other. It not only shuts out all other countries as far as possible from one particular market, but confines the colonies as far as possible to one particular market; and there is a great difference between being shut out of one market while all others are open, and being confined to one market while all others are closed. Yet the surplus produce of the colonies is the original source of all the increase in enjoyments and industry that Europe gains from the discovery and colonization of America, and the exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to make this source far less abundant than it would otherwise be.

before: It should be noted that England was a great trading country, with a very large mercantile capital that was likely to grow greater every day, not only before the Act of Navigation had set up the monopoly of the corn trade but before that trade was even very considerable. In the Dutch war, under Cromwell's government, her navy was superior to that of Holland; and in the war that broke out at the start of Charles II's reign, it was at least equal, perhaps superior, to the combined navies of France and Holland. Its superiority would scarcely look any greater in the present day, at least if the Dutch navy now bore the same proportion to Dutch commerce that it did then. But this great naval power could not, in either of those wars, have been owing to the Act of Navigation. During the first war, the plan of that act had only just been drawn up; and though it had been fully enacted by legal authority before the second war broke out, no part of it could have had time to produce any considerable effect, least of all the part that set up the exclusive trade to the colonies. Both the colonies and their trade were small then, compared with what they are now. The island of Jamaica was an unhealthy desert, little inhabited and still less cultivated. New York and New Jersey were in the hands of the Dutch, and half of St Christopher's in those of the French. The island of Antigua, the two Carolinas, Pennsylvania, Georgia, and Nova Scotia had not been settled. Virginia, Maryland, and New England were settled; and although they were very thriving colonies, there was perhaps not at that time, in Europe or America, a single person who foresaw, or even suspected, the rapid progress they have since made in wealth, population, and improvement. In short, the island of Barbados was the only British colony of any importance whose condition then bore any resemblance to what it is now. The trade of the colonies, of which England enjoyed only a part even for some time after the Act of Navigation (for that act was not very strictly enforced until several years after it was passed), could not at that time have been the cause of the great trade of England, nor of the great naval power that trade supported. The trade that supported that great naval power at the time was the trade of Europe and of the Mediterranean countries. But the share of that trade that Great Britain now enjoys could not support any such great naval power. Had the growing trade of the colonies been left open to all nations, then whatever share of it might have fallen to Great Britain, and a very considerable share probably would have, must all have been an addition to the great trade she already had. Because of the monopoly, the increase of the colony trade has not so much added to the trade Great Britain had before as completely changed its direction.

before: Every disturbance of the natural distribution of stock is necessarily harmful to the society in which it takes place, whether it drives away from a particular trade the stock that would otherwise go to it, or draws toward a particular trade stock that would not otherwise come to it. If, without any exclusive company, Holland's trade to the East Indies would be greater than it actually is, that country must suffer a considerable loss by having part of its capital shut out of the employment most convenient for that port. And in the same way, if, without an exclusive company, the trade of Sweden and Denmark to the East Indies would be less than it actually is, or, what is perhaps more likely, would not exist at all, those two countries must likewise suffer a considerable loss by having part of their capital drawn into an employment more or less unsuited to their present circumstances. It might be better for them, perhaps, as things now stand, to buy East India goods from other nations, even at a somewhat higher price, than to turn so large a part of their small capital to so very distant a trade, in which the returns are so very slow, in which that capital can support so little productive labour at home, where productive labour is so badly needed, where so little is done, and where so much is left to do.

before: To prevent export, the whole inland trade in wool is placed under very heavy and oppressive restrictions. Wool cannot be packed in any box, barrel, cask, case, chest, or other container, but only in packs of leather or pack-cloth, on which the word WOOL or YARN must be marked on the outside in large letters at least three inches long, on pain of forfeiting both the wool and the package, plus 8s for every pound weight, payable by the owner or packer. It cannot be loaded onto any horse or cart, or carried by land within five miles of the coast, except between sunrise and sunset, on pain of forfeiting the wool, the horses, and the carriages. The hundred next to the sea coast, out of or through which the wool is carried or exported, forfeits £20 if the wool is worth under £10, and if worth more, treble that value plus treble costs, to be sued for within the year. Enforcement falls on any two of the inhabitants, whom the sessions must repay through an assessment on the others, just as in cases of robbery. And if anyone settles with the hundred for less than this penalty, he is to be imprisoned for five years, and any other person may prosecute. These rules apply throughout the whole kingdom.

before: The old English East India Company was established in 1600 by a charter from Queen Elizabeth. In the first twelve voyages they fitted out for India they appear to have traded as a regulated company, with separate stocks, though only in the company's general ships. In 1612 they united into a joint stock. Their charter was exclusive, and, though not confirmed by act of parliament, was in those days supposed to convey a real exclusive privilege. For many years, therefore, they were not much troubled by interlopers. Their capital, which never exceeded £744,000, and of which £50 was a share, was not so excessive, nor their dealings so extensive, as to give either a pretext for gross negligence and extravagance or a cover for gross malversation. Despite some extraordinary losses, caused partly by the malice of the Dutch East India Company and partly by other accidents, they carried on a successful trade for many years. But in time, as the principles of liberty came to be better understood, it grew every day more and more doubtful how far a royal charter, not confirmed by act of parliament, could convey an exclusive privilege. On this question the decisions of the courts of justice were not uniform, but varied with the authority of government and the moods of the times. Interlopers multiplied against them, and towards the end of the reign of Charles II, throughout that of James II, and during part of that of William III, reduced them to great distress. In 1698 a proposal was made to parliament to advance two million to government at eight per cent, provided the subscribers were set up as a new East India company with exclusive privileges. The old East India Company offered seven hundred thousand pounds, nearly the whole of their capital, at four per cent on the same conditions. But such was the state of public credit at that time that it was more convenient for government to borrow two million at eight per cent than seven hundred thousand at four. The new subscribers' proposal was accepted, and a new East India company established as a result. The old company, however, had a right to continue their trade till 1701. They had, at the same time, very artfully subscribed three hundred and fifteen thousand pounds, in the name of their treasurer, into the stock of the new company. Through a careless wording of the act of parliament that vested the East India trade in the subscribers to this loan of two million, it did not clearly appear that they were all obliged to unite into a joint stock. A few private traders, whose subscriptions came to only seven thousand two hundred pounds, insisted on the privilege of trading separately on their own stocks and at their own risk. The old East India Company had a right to a separate trade on their own stock till 1701, and they also had, both before and after that date, a right, like that of other private traders, to a separate trade on the £315,000 they had subscribed into the stock of the new company. The competition of the two companies with the private traders, and with one another, is said to have very nearly ruined both. On a later occasion, in 1730, when a proposal was made to parliament to put the trade under the management of a regulated company, and thereby in some measure open it up, the East India Company, opposing this proposal, described in very strong terms what they thought had been the miserable effects of this competition at that time. In India, they said, it raised the price of goods so high that they were not worth buying; and in England, by overstocking the market, it sank their price so low that no profit could be made by them. That a more plentiful supply, to the great advantage and convenience of the public, must have greatly reduced the price of India goods in the English market cannot well be doubted; but that it should have greatly raised their price in the Indian market seems not very likely, since all the extra demand that competition could cause must have been but as a drop of water in the immense ocean of Indian commerce. Besides, an increase of demand, though it may sometimes raise the price of goods at first, never fails to lower it in the long run. It encourages production, and thereby increases the competition of the producers, who, in order to undersell one another, resort to new divisions of labour and new improvements of art that might otherwise never have been thought of. The miserable effects of which the company complained were cheaper consumption and the encouragement given to production, precisely the two effects which it is the great business of political economy to promote. The competition, however, of which they gave this doleful account had not been allowed to last long. In 1702 the two companies were in some measure united by a tripartite indenture, to which the queen was the third party; and in 1708 they were by act of parliament perfectly consolidated into one company, under their present name of the United Company of Merchants Trading to the East Indies. It was thought worth while to insert into this act a clause allowing the separate traders to continue their trade till Michaelmas 1711, but at the same time empowering the directors, on three years' notice, to buy out their little capital of seven thousand two hundred pounds, and thereby turn the whole stock of the company into a joint stock. By the same act, the company's capital, in consequence of a new loan to government, was raised from two million to three million two hundred thousand pounds. In 1743 the company advanced another million to government. But since this million was raised not by a call on the proprietors but by selling annuities and contracting bond debts, it did not increase the stock on which the proprietors could claim a dividend. It did, however, increase their trading stock, being equally liable with the other three million two hundred thousand pounds for the losses sustained, and debts contracted, by the company in pursuing their mercantile projects. From 1708, or at least from 1711, this company, freed from all competitors and fully established in the monopoly of the English trade to the East Indies, carried on a successful trade, and out of their profits made their proprietors a moderate dividend every year. During the French war that began in 1741, the ambition of Mr Dupleix, the French governor of Pondicherry, drew them into the wars of the Carnatic and into the politics of the Indian princes. After many signal successes and equally signal losses, they at last lost Madras, at that time their principal settlement in India. It was restored to them by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, and about this time the spirit of war and conquest seems to have taken hold of their servants in India, and never since to have left them. During the French war that began in 1755, their arms shared in the general good fortune of those of Great Britain. They defended Madras, took Pondicherry, recovered Calcutta, and acquired the revenues of a rich and extensive territory, amounting, it was then said, to upwards of three million a year. They remained for several years in quiet possession of this revenue; but in 1767 the administration laid claim to their territorial acquisitions, and the revenue arising from them, as of right belonging to the crown; and the company, in compensation for this claim, agreed to pay government £400,000 a year. Before this they had gradually raised their dividend from about six to ten per cent; that is, on their capital of three million two hundred thousand pounds they had increased it by £128,000, or raised it from one hundred and ninety-two thousand to three hundred and twenty thousand pounds a year. About this time they were attempting to raise it still further, to twelve and a half per cent, which would have made their annual payments to their proprietors equal to what they had agreed to pay government every year, or £400,000 a year. But during the two years in which their agreement with government was to take effect, they were restrained from any further increase of dividend by two successive acts of parliament, the aim of which was to enable them to make faster progress in paying off their debts, which were at this time estimated at upwards of six or seven million sterling. In 1769 they renewed their agreement with government for five years more, and stipulated that during that period they should be allowed gradually to raise their dividend to twelve and a half per cent, never increasing it, however, by more than one per cent in a year. So this increase of dividend, when it had risen to its utmost height, could add but £680,000 to their annual payments, to their proprietors and government together, beyond what they had been before their late territorial acquisitions. What the gross revenue of those territorial acquisitions was supposed to amount to has already been mentioned; and by an account brought by the Cruttenden East Indiaman in 1769, the net revenue, clear of all deductions and military charges, was put at two million forty-eight thousand seven hundred and forty-seven pounds. They were said at the same time to have another revenue, arising partly from lands but chiefly from the customs established at their various settlements, amounting to £439,000. The profits of their trade, too, according to the evidence of their chairman before the House of Commons, came at this time to at least £400,000 a year; according to that of their accountant, to at least £500,000; on the lowest account, at least equal to the highest dividend that was to be paid to their proprietors. So great a revenue might certainly have afforded an increase of £680,000 in their annual payments and, at the same time, have left a large sinking fund, enough for the speedy reduction of their debt. In 1773, however, their debts, instead of being reduced, were increased by an arrear to the Treasury in paying the four hundred thousand pounds; by another to the custom house for unpaid duties; by a large debt to the bank for money borrowed; and by a fourth, for bills drawn on them from India and recklessly accepted, to the amount of upwards of twelve hundred thousand pounds. The distress these accumulated claims brought on them obliged them not only to cut their dividend all at once to six per cent, but to throw themselves on the mercy of government, and to beg, first, a release from any further payment of the stipulated £400,000 a year, and second, a loan of fourteen hundred thousand to save them from immediate bankruptcy. The great increase of their fortune had, it seems, only served to furnish their servants with a pretext for greater extravagance, and a cover for greater malversation, than even in proportion to that increase of fortune. The conduct of their servants in India, and the general state of their affairs both in India and in Europe, became the subject of a parliamentary inquiry, in consequence of which several very important changes were made in the constitution of their government, both at home and abroad. In India, their principal settlements of Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta, which had before been wholly independent of one another, were placed under a governor-general assisted by a council of four assessors, parliament taking to itself the first nomination of this governor and council, who were to reside at Calcutta, that city having now become, what Madras had been before, the most important of the English settlements in India. The court of the Mayor of Calcutta, originally set up to try mercantile cases arising in the city and neighbourhood, had gradually extended its jurisdiction as the empire spread. It was now cut back and confined to the original purpose of its institution. In its place a new supreme court of judicature was established, consisting of a chief justice and three judges, to be appointed by the crown. In Europe, the qualification needed to entitle a proprietor to vote at their general courts was raised from five hundred pounds, the original price of a share in the company's stock, to a thousand pounds. To vote on this qualification, too, it was declared necessary that he should have held it, if acquired by his own purchase and not by inheritance, for at least one year, instead of the six months required before. The court of twenty-four directors had before been chosen annually; but it was now enacted that each director should in future be chosen for four years, six of them, however, to leave office by rotation every year, and not be eligible for re-election at the choosing of the six new directors for the following year. In consequence of these changes, the courts both of the proprietors and of the directors were expected to act with more dignity and steadiness than they usually had before. But it seems impossible, by any changes, to make those courts in any way fit to govern, or even to share in the government of, a great empire, because most of their members must always have too little interest in the prosperity of that empire to give any serious attention to what may promote it. Frequently a man of great fortune, sometimes even one of small fortune, is willing to buy a thousand-pound share in India stock merely for the influence he expects to gain by a vote in the court of proprietors. It gives him a share, not indeed in the plunder, but in the appointment of the plunderers of India; for the court of directors, though they make that appointment, are necessarily more or less under the influence of the proprietors, who not only elect those directors but sometimes overrule the appointments of their servants in India. Provided he can enjoy this influence for a few years, and thereby provide for a certain number of his friends, he frequently cares little about the dividend, or even about the value of the stock on which his vote is founded. About the prosperity of the great empire in whose government that vote gives him a share, he seldom cares at all. No other sovereigns ever were, or, from the nature of things, ever could be, so perfectly indifferent about the happiness or misery of their subjects, the improvement or waste of their dominions, the glory or disgrace of their administration, as, from irresistible moral causes, most of the proprietors of such a mercantile company are, and necessarily must be. This indifference, too, was more likely to be increased than lessened by some of the new regulations made in consequence of the parliamentary inquiry. By a resolution of the House of Commons, for example, it was declared that when the £1,400,000 lent to the company by government should be paid, and their bond debts reduced to £1,500,000, they might then, and not till then, divide eight per cent on their capital; and that whatever remained of their revenues and net profits at home should be divided into four parts, three of them to be paid into the Exchequer for the use of the public, and the fourth to be kept as a fund either for the further reduction of their bond debts or for meeting other contingent needs the company might labour under. But if the company were bad stewards and bad sovereigns when the whole of their net revenue and profits belonged to themselves and were at their own disposal, they were surely not likely to be better when three-fourths of it were to belong to other people, and the other fourth, though to be spent for the company's benefit, yet to be so under the inspection and with the approval of other people.

before: Even when such taxes are set in proportion to the value of the property transferred, they are still unequal, because property of equal value does not always change hands equally often. When they are not proportioned to that value, which is true of most stamp duties and registration duties, they are more unequal still. In no respect are they arbitrary; they are, or can be, perfectly clear and certain in every case. Although they sometimes fall on someone not well able to pay, the moment of payment is in most cases convenient enough for him, since when the tax falls due he will usually have the more to pay it with. They are collected at very little expense and generally subject those who pay them to no inconvenience beyond the unavoidable one of paying. before: In the first book I tried to show that the wages of the lower classes of workers are everywhere necessarily governed by two things: the demand for labour and the ordinary or average price of food and other provisions. Whether the demand for labour is rising, steady, or falling, and whether it calls for a growing, steady, or shrinking population, determines how the labourer is provided for and whether his subsistence is generous, modest, or meagre. The ordinary average price of provisions then determines how much money he must be paid to buy that generous, modest, or meagre subsistence, year in and year out. So long as the demand for labour and the price of provisions stay the same, a direct tax on wages can do nothing but push wages somewhat higher than the tax itself. Suppose, for example, that in some place the demand for labour and the price of provisions made ten shillings a week the ordinary wage, and that a tax of one-fifth, or four shillings in the pound, was laid on wages. If the demand for labour and the price of provisions stayed the same, the labourer would still need to earn enough to buy a subsistence that cost ten shillings a week, so that after paying the tax he would have ten shillings a week left as free wages. But to leave him those free wages after such a tax, the price of labour in that place must soon rise not just to twelve shillings a week but to twelve shillings and sixpence: that is, to let him pay a tax of one-fifth, his wages must soon rise not by a fifth but by a quarter. Whatever the proportion of the tax, wages must in every case rise not merely in that proportion but in a higher one. If the tax were a tenth, for instance, wages must soon rise not by a tenth but by an eighth.

before: The bounties sometimes paid on the export of home produce and manufactures, and the drawbacks paid on the re-export of most foreign goods, have given rise to many frauds and to a kind of smuggling more destructive of the public revenue than any other. To collect the bounty or drawback, the goods are—as is well known—sometimes shipped and sent to sea, then soon afterwards secretly landed again in some other part of the country. The loss of customs revenue caused by bounties and drawbacks, a large part of which are obtained by fraud, is very great. The gross customs revenue in the year that ended on 5 January 1755 came to £5,068,000. The bounties paid out of this revenue, even though there was no corn bounty that year, came to £167,806. The drawbacks paid on debentures and certificates came to £2,156,800. Bounties and drawbacks together came to £2,324,600. After these deductions the customs revenue amounted to only £2,743,400; and after deducting £287,900 for the cost of management—salaries and other incidentals—the net customs revenue for that year works out at £2,455,500. The cost of management thus amounts to between five and six per cent of the gross customs revenue, and to something more than ten per cent of what is left after deducting what is paid out in bounties and drawbacks.

before: Since heavy duties are imposed on almost everything imported, our importing merchants smuggle as much as they can and declare as little as they can. Our exporting merchants, on the other hand, declare more than they actually export—sometimes out of vanity, to pass as great dealers in goods that pay no duty, and sometimes to claim a bounty on goods that paid duty on import and now earn the duty back. Because of these various frauds, our exports appear in the custom-house books to outweigh our imports by a wide margin, to the boundless satisfaction of those politicians who measure the nation's prosperity by what they call the balance of trade.

before: All imported goods, unless specifically exempted—and such exemptions are not very numerous—are subject to some customs duties. If goods are imported that are not listed in the book of rates, they are taxed at 4s 9¾ d for every twenty shillings of value, according to the importer's sworn declaration—that is, at nearly five subsidies, or five poundage duties. The book of rates is extremely comprehensive and lists a great variety of articles, many of them little used and therefore not well known. For this reason it is often unclear under which heading a particular kind of goods should be classed, and consequently what duty it should pay. before: During Queen Anne's reign the market rate of interest had fallen from six to five per cent, and in the twelfth year of her reign five per cent was declared the highest rate that could lawfully be taken for money borrowed on private security. Soon after most of Great Britain's temporary taxes had been made perpetual and distributed among the aggregate, South Sea, and general funds, the public creditors, like those of private persons, were induced to accept five per cent interest on their money. This saved one per cent on the capital of most of the debts funded in perpetuity, or one-sixth of most of the annuities paid out of the three great funds just mentioned. This saving left a considerable surplus in the produce of the various taxes gathered into those funds, beyond what was needed to pay the annuities now charged on them, and laid the foundation of what has since been called the sinking fund. In 1717 it came to £523,454 7s 7½d. In 1727 the interest on most of the public debts was further reduced to four per cent, and in 1753 and 1757 to three and a half and three per cent—reductions that increased the sinking fund still further.

before: During the reigns of King William and Queen Anne, large sums were often borrowed on annuities for terms of years, sometimes longer and sometimes shorter. In 1695 an act was passed to borrow one million on an annuity of fourteen per cent, or £140,000 a year, for sixteen years. In 1691 an act was passed to borrow a million on annuities for lives, on terms that would seem very advantageous today, but the subscription was not filled. The next year the shortfall was made good by borrowing on annuities for lives at fourteen per cent, a little more than seven years' purchase. In 1695 the people who had bought those annuities were allowed to exchange them for ninety-six-year annuities by paying sixty-three pounds in the hundred into the exchequer; that is, the difference between fourteen per cent for life and fourteen per cent for ninety-six years was sold for sixty-three pounds, or four and a half years' purchase. Such was the supposed instability of the government that even these terms found few buyers. In Queen Anne's reign, money was borrowed on various occasions both on annuities for lives and on annuities for terms of thirty-two, eighty-nine, ninety-eight, and ninety-nine years. In 1719 the holders of the thirty-two-year annuities were induced to accept, in their place, South Sea stock worth eleven and a half years' purchase of the annuities, together with an extra amount of stock equal to the arrears then due on them. In 1720 most of the other annuities for terms of years, both long and short, were subscribed into the same fund. The long annuities at that time came to £666,821 8s 3½d a year. On 5 January 1775 the remainder of them, or what had not been subscribed at that time, came to only £136,453 12s 8d.

before: Under Mr Pelham's administration the interest on the public debt was reduced—or at least steps were taken to reduce it—from four to three per cent; the sinking fund was increased, and some of the public debt was paid off. In 1755, before the late war broke out, the funded debt of Great Britain came to £72,289,675. On 5 January 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, the funded debt came to £122,603,336 8s 2¼d.
